en: *The Treatise on the Determination of Names and Meanings in All Teachings*,
composed by the Holy Bodhisattva Maitreya;
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao Feng Da Fu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.
I take refuge in all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; I take refuge in the Dharma of the Three Vehicles as they have been taught;
I take refuge in the entire Saṃgha of harmonious assembly; I take refuge in the principle of Samantabhadra’s Dharmadhātu.
Now, I shall briefly explain the fundamental syllables within all teachings.
What is their meaning as it truly is?
It is as follows:
The syllable Oṃ is the foremost.
I now prostrate to this syllable, which dwells in purity within the non-dual state.
Furthermore, if there be anyone who can cause this syllable to revolve upon their tongue, they shall attain the root of all true wisdom.
This syllable is profoundly secret within all teachings. Furthermore, there are three syllables;

namely, the Vajra HŪṂ syllable serves as the primary cause. From this syllable, the ritual procedures for all the true dharmas are proclaimed. The mind of those in the three realms is such that it conforms to this dharma.
The syllable *A* explains the characteristic of appearance; the syllable *Am* is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

That very syllable *A* is further the mother of wisdom (*prajñā*); whether it be the path or not the path, all is explained from this. It is also the root of the syllables of the *dharmadhātu*, pervading and entering emptiness in correspondence from beginning to end; through this correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), accomplishment is attained.
If all dharmas that have been taught are fully accomplished, so too is that which has not been taught.
Therefore, all conditioned activities are entirely equal, revolving in accordance with the cycle of saṃsāra.
Regarding what was said about the words of the Dharma-realm,
how is this so? Therefore, it is now explained as follows:
Ka-kha-ga-ṅa-ca-cha-ja-jha-ña-ṭa-ṭha-ḍa-ḍha-ṇa-ta-tha-da-dha-na-pa-pha-ba-bha-ma-ya-ra-la-va-śa-ṣa-sa-ha.
All such syllables are subsumed within that syllable *Aṃ*, as previously explained.
This characteristic is now described: it is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which gives rise to all profound teachings; this, moreover, is called "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).
All the signs of speech appear, namely: ka kha ga gha ṅa; ca cha ja jha ña; ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa; ta tha da dha na; pa pha ba bha ma; ya ra la va; śa ṣa sa ha.
These syllables are as previously described, being subsumed within those "evil" syllables.

Their characteristics are now explained: namely, that each and every syllable arises from the initial corresponding practice of the wisdom of omniscience; both the self and phenomena are entirely equal, and they abide ultimately through the empowerment of the Vajra.
Furthermore, all ritual activities arise from the Vajra-samādhi. They are as follows:
KA KHA GA GHA CA CHA JA JHA ÑA ṬA ṬHA ḌA ḌHA ṆA TA THA DA DHA NA PA PHA BA BHA YA RA LA VA ŚA ṢA SA HA.
Thus, all these syllables are subsumed within the long vowel Ā.
This characteristic is now explained as being all vajra activities.
Furthermore, it is now said:

U (pronounced like *wu* with the *u* of *wu-gong*); Wu (pronounced like *wu* with the *u* of *wu-gong*); Yi (pronounced like *yi-ling*); Yi (pronounced like *yi-zheng*); Li (pronounced like *li-ding*, same for the following); Li (pronounced like *li-li*, same for the following); Li (pronounced like *yi-yi-ling*); Ai (pronounced like *yi-gang*); Oṃ (pronounced like *wu-long*); Āḥ (pronounced like *wu-dang*).
Regarding the form of the syllable Oṃ herein, it is now explained as follows: that is to say, all letters are produced from it.
Regarding the form of the syllable Hūṃ herein, it is as previously stated: all ritual activities are produced from the Vajra-samādhi.
Furthermore, regarding the syllables previously mentioned, they are the three bodies (trikāya), abiding in their true nature and characteristics as they are.
Namely: the syllable HŪṂ is the Dharmakāya; the syllable A is the Saṃbhogakāya; and the syllable OṂ is the Nirmāṇakāya.
These three syllables encompass these three bodies (*trikāya*).
Their detailed exposition of the path to liberation for the three vehicles (*triyāna*) constitutes the cause of correct teaching.
All *śrāvakas*, *pratyekabuddhas*, and the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) emerge from this; thus it is said that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are taught thereby.
Those three syllables are likewise the vajra three-karma abiding in accordance with reality.
They are: Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ.
In this context, the syllable Oṃ is called the vajra body activity; the syllable Ā is the vajra speech activity; and the syllable Hūṃ is the vajra mind activity.
Furthermore, the two syllables Ā and Aḥ abide in emptiness; herein, the syllable Aḥ is also correct wisdom, and herein, the syllable Ā is the supreme secret of perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, the syllable *HŪṂ* constitutes the mind of wisdom (*cittajñāna*), through which all phenomena are realized.

One should know that all the aforementioned syllables arise from these three syllables—*AṂ*, *ĀḤ*, and *HŪṂ*. From these, the various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena arise; these shall now be analyzed.

All those phenomena are encompassed by the initial and final aspects of the two syllables *Aṃ* and *Āḥ*. Within this, the syllable *Hūṃ* gives birth to all things, manifesting various forms within the three realms. All devas, humans, nāgas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, gandharvas; the accomplished vidyādharīs, Śrī-devī, Sarasvatī-devī, Umā-devī; Śakra-deva, Brahmā-deva, Nārāyaṇa-deva, Maheśvara-deva—such devas and their consorts—as well as all male and female beings within the realm of sentient beings, even down to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, are all born from and transformed by this syllable *Hūṃ*. Each and every mind abides in the aspect of this syllable.

If one contemplates this syllable in the mind, one shall abide in space and give rise to non-obstruction; that is to say, the minds of the three realms are identical to this single mind and enter therein.
Having entered this mind, this is called the direct realization of enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*).

One should know that this mind is without equal and without grasping, without attachment and without dwelling, without expression and without characteristics; it is the all-knowledge (sarvajñā) that is equal to space.
It is the practice of correct conduct that accords with non-apprehension and accords with the absence of self and other.

All the various modes of conduct of those in the lowest castes, such as the caṇḍālas and others in this world, as well as the various distinct modes of conduct of even the animal species and so forth.
Although these various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) differ from one another, none of them is apart from the correct practice associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Furthermore, it is said that the nature of all syllables and words does not exist; nevertheless, that knowledge of all modes is skillfully proclaimed through all syllables and words.
In this context, what is the meaning of "syllables"?
It means the meaning of space (*ākāśa*).
What is the meaning of space?
This refers to the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). What is the meaning of emptiness?
It is the meaning of *śūnya*.
What is the meaning of *śūnyatā*?
It means the absence of anything to be expressed.
What is the meaning of the absence of anything to be expressed?
This refers to the meaning of signlessness.
What is the meaning of signlessness?
It is the meaning of omniscience.
What is the meaning of "omniscience"?
It means the meaning of the wish-fulfilling gem.
What is the meaning of the "wish-fulfilling gem"?
This refers to the meaning of "knowledge" (jñāna).
Furthermore, what is the meaning of knowledge?
It is the meaning of "mind" (citta).
Furthermore, what is the meaning of "mind" (*citta*)?
It refers to the sense of great sovereignty over the three realms.
What is the meaning of great sovereignty over the three realms?
It means the sense of universal illumination.
What is the meaning of universal illumination?
It means the sense of Brahmā.
What is the meaning of "Brahmā"?
It means the sense of a "Great Powerful Deva.
What is the meaning of a "Great Powerful Deva"?
This refers to the meaning of Īśvara.
What is the meaning of Īśvara?
It is precisely the meaning of Buddha.
What is the meaning of "Buddha"?
It means the meaning of Vajrasattva.
What is the meaning of Vajrasattva?
It refers to the meaning of Avalokiteśvara.
What is the meaning of Avalokiteśvara?
It refers to the meaning of the world.
What is the meaning of "the world"?
It means the meaning of saṃsāra.
What is the meaning of saṃsāra?
It refers to the meaning of *nirvāṇa*.
What is the meaning of *nirvāṇa*?
It is the meaning of being incalculable.
What is the meaning of "incalculable"?
It means that which cannot be known.
What is the meaning of "cannot be known"?
This refers to the meaning of non-arising.
What is the meaning of non-arising?
It refers to the meaning of non-ceasing.
What is the meaning of "non-extinction"?
It means the meaning of "formlessness.
What is the meaning of "formlessness"?
This means there is no meaning of sound.
What is the meaning of "no sound"?
It means there is no fundamental meaning.
What is the meaning of "having no root"?
It means having no sense of nourishment.
What is the meaning of "no nourishment"?
This refers to the meaning of non-abiding.
What is the meaning of non-abiding?

This non-abiding is that which is nothing whatsoever; it is free from all existence, knowledge, conceptualization, and discrimination; it transcends all Buddhas and the Bodhi of the Buddhas, and abides securely in the fundamental Vajra HŪṂ syllable.

This very syllable HŪṂ further becomes a lotus-fire maṇḍala, abiding in the two fundamental, supreme, and utterly pure correspondences: the nature of emptiness within emptiness and the dharmatā free from dust.
Having understood this, one should apply courageous diligence within saṃsāra so that all may universally attain the great bliss of nirvāṇa.

If one abides in this mind, it is the method for the wise to extinguish suffering and affliction; since both types of roots are entirely equal, this is the supreme practice of diligence that accomplishes the Great Bliss Dharma of the Muni, abiding in right mindfulness.
Just as the light of the sun shines universally upon the world, the mind and wisdom abide in equal correspondence.
All that is profound and secret, as previously described—including the *śūṣira* and the division of space—is likewise explained in this way.

Thus, by accomplishing this Dharma of supreme bliss, one attains correspondence with the self-nature of all Buddhas. One should understand that all sentient beings in the world, and all phenomena of birth, consist of the union and correspondence of the two types of craving—existence and non-existence—and are devoid of intrinsic nature; these impermanent phenomena are ultimately empty and quiescent.
